nodes.label: Work, Energy and Power
nodes.note: Mechanical work, the work-energy theorem, conservation of energy, potential curves, and power. JEE tests variable forces, friction dissipation, equilibrium stability, and constant power kinematics.

nodes.label: Mechanical Work
nodes.note: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement. It can be positive, negative, or zero depending on the angle between force and displacement.

nodes.label: Work by Constant Force
nodes.note: For a constant force, $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s} = Fs\cos\theta$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle between force and displacement. The SI unit is the joule: $$[W] = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$$.

nodes.label: Dimensions and Units
nodes.note: Work has dimensions $$[M L^2 T^{-2}]$$. $$1\text{ J} = 10^7\text{ erg}$$. The CGS unit of work is the erg.

nodes.label: Work by Variable Force
nodes.note: For a variable force along a path $$C$$: $$W = \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int F_x\,dx + \int F_y\,dy + \int F_z\,dz$$.

nodes.label: Area Under F-x Curve
nodes.note: The work done by a 1D variable force equals the signed area between the $$F$$-$$x$$ curve and the displacement axis: $$W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$$.

nodes.label: Sign of Work
nodes.note: Positive work ($$0 \le \theta < 90^\circ$$) transfers energy into the body. Negative work ($$90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$$) extracts energy. Zero work occurs when $$\theta = 90^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Zero Work Cases
nodes.note: Zero work occurs when force is perpendicular to displacement: centripetal force in circular motion, magnetic Lorentz force $$q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$$, and normal reaction on a fixed surface.

nodes.label: Work by Canonical Forces
nodes.note: Gravity, spring force, and internal tension have standard work formulas that appear repeatedly in JEE problems.

nodes.label: Gravitational Work
nodes.note: Near Earth's surface, $$W_g = -mg\Delta y = mg(y_i - y_f)$$. Gravitational work depends only on initial and final vertical coordinates, not on the path taken.

nodes.label: Spring Work
nodes.note: For an ideal spring, $$W_s = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2) = -\Delta U_s$$. The work done by a spring equals the negative change in spring potential energy.

nodes.label: Internal Tension Work
nodes.note: For an ideal string connecting multiple masses, internal tension transfers energy without net work: $$\sum W_T = \sum \vec{T} \cdot d\vec{s} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Friction and Energy
nodes.note: Static friction does zero net work on a system; kinetic friction always dissipates mechanical energy as heat.

nodes.label: Static Friction Work
nodes.note: Static friction can do positive, negative, or zero work on an individual body. But across the entire interacting system, the net work is identically zero: $$\sum W_{f_s} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Static Friction Work Cases
nodes.note: A crate accelerating in a truck bed: static friction does positive work. A person walking: the contact foot has zero displacement, so $$W_{f_s} = 0$$. Static friction never dissipates energy.

nodes.label: Kinetic Friction Dissipation
nodes.note: When two bodies slide with relative displacement $$s_{\text{rel}}$$, the net work of kinetic friction is strictly negative: $$\sum W_{f_k} = -f_k s_{\text{rel}} < 0$$.

nodes.label: Heat Generation
nodes.note: The lost mechanical energy becomes thermal energy: $$Q_{\text{heat}} = f_k s_{\text{rel}}$$. This dissipation is irreversible and independent of the friction coefficient.

nodes.label: Frame Dependence of Work
nodes.note: Work is frame-dependent because displacement changes: $$W' = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}' \ne W$$. However, the work-energy theorem $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$$ holds in every inertial frame.

nodes.label: Work-Energy Theorem
nodes.note: The net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy. This is the cornerstone of energy methods in mechanics.

nodes.label: Work-Energy Theorem
nodes.note: The net work equals the change in kinetic energy: $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2$$.

nodes.label: WET Derivation
nodes.note: From $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$$: $$W_{\text{net}} = \int m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} \cdot \vec{v}\,dt = \int m\vec{v} \cdot d\vec{v} = \left[\frac{1}{2}mv^2\right]_{v_i}^{v_f}$$.

nodes.label: Force Partitioning
nodes.note: Partitioning work into conservative, non-conservative, and external parts: $$W_C + W_{\text{NC}} + W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta K$$. Since $$W_C = -\Delta U$$, this gives $$W_{\text{NC}} + W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta E_{\text{mech}}$$.

nodes.label: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
nodes.note: If only conservative forces do work, mechanical energy is conserved: $$\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = 0 \iff K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f = \text{constant}$$.

nodes.label: Conservative Fields
nodes.note: A force field is conservative if its work is path-independent or equivalently if it can be derived from a scalar potential.

nodes.label: Curl Condition
nodes.note: A force field is conservative if and only if $$\vec{\nabla} \times \vec{F} = \vec{0}$$. This is the irrotational condition.

nodes.label: Force from Potential
nodes.note: A conservative force is the negative gradient of potential energy: $$\vec{F} = -\vec{\nabla}U = -\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Potential Energy Curves
nodes.note: The $$U(x)$$ curve reveals force, equilibrium stability, and allowed regions of motion.

nodes.label: Force-Potential Gradient
nodes.note: In one dimension, $$F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$$. The force points toward decreasing potential energy.

nodes.label: Equilibrium Stability
nodes.note: Equilibrium occurs where $$\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$$. The second derivative determines stability.

nodes.label: Stable Equilibrium
nodes.note: At a local minimum ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$$), the force is restoring. The particle executes SHM with $$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Unstable Equilibrium
nodes.note: At a local maximum ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$$), the force reinforces displacement. The particle accelerates away from equilibrium.

nodes.label: Neutral Equilibrium
nodes.note: On a flat plateau ($$\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 0$$), the force remains zero. The particle stays at rest in its new position.

nodes.label: Classical Turning Points
nodes.note: Since $$K(x) = E - U(x) \ge 0$$, motion is confined to $$U(x) \le E$$. Turning points occur where $$U(x_t) = E$$ and the particle reverses direction.

nodes.label: Allowed and Forbidden Regions
nodes.note: The allowed region is where $$U(x) \le E$$. Regions where $$U(x) > E$$ would require negative kinetic energy and are classically forbidden.

nodes.label: Power
nodes.note: Power is the rate of doing work. Constant power motion has distinctive kinematic scaling laws.

nodes.label: Instantaneous Power
nodes.note: Instantaneous power is $$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = Fv\cos\theta$$. Net power equals the rate of change of kinetic energy: $$P_{\text{net}} = \frac{dK}{dt}$$.

nodes.label: Average Power
nodes.note: Average power is $$P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t} = \frac{W_{\text{total}}}{\Delta t}$$.

nodes.label: Motion Under Constant Power
nodes.note: An engine delivering constant power $$P$$ to a vehicle of mass $$m$$ from rest produces characteristic scaling laws.

nodes.label: Velocity Scaling
nodes.note: From $$P = mv\frac{dv}{dt}$$: $$v(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}}\,t^{1/2} \propto t^{1/2}$$.

nodes.label: Displacement Scaling
nodes.note: Integrating velocity: $$x(t) = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}}\,t^{3/2} \propto t^{3/2}$$. Acceleration decreases as $$a = \frac{P}{mv} \propto t^{-1/2}$$.

nodes.label: Advanced Applications
nodes.note: Hanging chain work and conveyor belt mechanics involve continuous mass redistribution and energy dissipation.

nodes.label: Hanging Chain Work
nodes.note: For a uniform chain of mass $$M$$ and length $$L$$ with fraction $$1/n$$ hanging, the work to pull it up is $$W = \frac{MgL}{2n^2}$$. This uses the center of mass of the hanging segment.

nodes.label: Conveyor Belt 50% Law
nodes.note: Sand falling on a conveyor belt moving at speed $$v$$: motor power is $$P_{\text{motor}} = v^2\frac{dm}{dt}$$. Exactly 50% becomes kinetic energy; 50% is dissipated as heat.
